speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I hold in my hand a copy of the Winnipeg Free Press of last Wednesday afternoon, February 29. On page 5 I find the report of a speech made in the provincial legislature by Premier Campbell of my province, from which I should like to read just two sentences. My point of privilege is that they reflect on this house and on an important section of the staff of this house. The first sentence reads:
Premier D. L. Campbell Tuesday objected to a proposal to have a provincial Hansard (a written record of legislative debate) on the grounds that abuses would result.
The next sentence is in quotation marks, and it is attributed to Premier Campbell.
"It is not understood the extent to which the Ottawa Hansard is doctored."
Apart from the fact that my friend the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), and others will not like the use of the word "doctored", I submit, Mr. Speaker, that all members know that any attempt to alter the meaning of anything said in this house is promptly frustrated, thanks in part at any rate to press publicity given to such efforts. The fact is that our Hansard staff produces a faithful record of what is said here and on their behalf, and as a member of the house, I object to Premier Campbell's words.
I have never heard Premier Campbell complaining of the record of the speeches he makes here in Ottawa when he attends federal-provincial conferences. Since it is our staff which records his speeches on those occasions, he should have known better than to make this unfounded charge.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING OWNED, OPERATED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the work done or, at any rate, intended to be done by this committee is important. I think it is one of the really important committees of the year. However, in the brief remarks that I intend to make this afternoon I wish to make some suggestions very earnestly as to one or two ways in which I think the work of the committee can be very greatly improved.
I want to picture to the house exactly what happens. The committee is appointed. Then we are notified that the railway officials will be here. Then they come and we receive the annual report. We have the president and the other railway officials there to assist us in understanding the report, to answer any questions which we ask, and in that they are extremely good and extremely obliging. Then probably within the course of the first day we are asked to approve very substantial capital expenditures.

I think it is really a responsibility which no committee, certainly a committee which does not pretend to be a committee of accounting experts, should be asked to undertake on such short notice. While, as I said, the railway officials are always extremely gracious and obliging, nevertheless there is a sense of urgency, a sense that they are busy men and we must not keep them an extra day because they have important things to do elsewhere and therefore we must be as sparing as we can in the use of their time.
I am not suggesting that is unreasonable. I am only suggesting that, if the members of the committee are completely honest with themselves, I do not believe that at the end of the day they really feel that they have grasped the situation and that they have approved the expenditure of money as if it were their own money. In my opinion, only if we were able to do that would we be discharging our duty, and I suggest very earnestly that as things are managed now we just cannot do that.
I speak frankly for myself. I do not feel happy at the end of the day that I have grasped the full situation and I am sure there would be others who would say the same thing. The president of the railway himself spoke about the railway accounts as a "statistician's dream". I think we know what he meant by that and, indeed, it is no disrespect to the operating officials of the railway to say that occasionally they more or less throw up their hands and say well, that is a technical matter, that is a difficult accounting matter, and we will have to ask the chief accountant to explain that to you. The reason I am saying this is that I want to make one or two suggestions which I cannot believe would be difficult to carry out and which I think would enable this committee to function much better, in my opinion, than it is now functioning.
In the first place I should like to suggest that these accounts should be given to us some days in advance, not the morning of the day we are asked to probe them. I think it would be much better if we could have them some time in advance. In the second place, I think it would be much better if we could have some assistance in advance from technicians, accountants and others. We need not have the chief accountant. I am quite sure that over in the Department of Finance or the Department of Transport there are other people who could give us a great deal of help if only we had the necessary time.
I therefore repeat that suggestion with great earnestness and, unless there are some strong reasons, against it, I hope it will be
Committee on Railways and Shipping adopted. I cannot believe that there are any such reasons. As the situation is now, we pass this resolution, the committee is set up and then suddenly one day we are told that the railway people will be here in the course of a day or two. They come up here, horse, foot and artillery, with all their staff and their papers and documents.
I wish to pursue this matter a little bit further. I wish the house to realize that what we are doing sometimes is to approve extremely large capital expenditures. Sometimes those expenditures are as the result of legislation passed in this house for the construction of this or that addition to the railway. I think we may as well face the fact that sometimes we dump into the lap of the Canadian National Railways management pieces of railway that are extremely difficult for them to operate and as to which, if they were as free as are their brethren in the C.P.R., they would perhaps say, "Don't let us have them".
I suggest another thing. When it happens that we have voted a substantial amount of money for this or that line, at the first opportunity after that line is in operation, when there is a chance to find out, as far as accountants can show us, just what has happened as a result of the building of the line, I think it would be a useful lesson for us and for this house to have these figures.
I am glad to note that progress is being made on the accounting side. I have expressed disappointment in the past because the surest test of all has not been available to us, the test that I should have liked and the one which I am sure will spring to the mind of everybody as the best test of all; viz., how do you compare with the C.P.R.? We have not been able to get that information in any satisfactory form. Indeed, I think I am not exaggerating when I say that we just have not obtained it. For that reason I am glad to observe that pursuant, I believe, to the recommendations of the Turgeon commission of some years ago, there was published last autumn under the authority of the board of transport commissioners what is called "Uniform Classification of Accounts". It is dated September, 1955, and is effective January 1.
In the foreword to this statement it is interesting to note that in 1939 a uniform accounting committee was appointed by Right Hon. C. D. Howe, then minister of transport; but because of more pressing problems arising from the outbreak of the world war the matter was put over until after the close of hostilities. Some time has gone by since then, and I am glad to see that we now have this "Uniform Classification of Accounts". I understand
1840	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping that from now on we shall have identical forms of keeping accounts and that we shall be able to compare them.
The chief changes, I understand-and this appeared in the press some little time ago-is that the Canadian National Railways is to be asked to alter its form of depreciation. I understand it depreciated rolling stock but did not depreciate track and buildings, treating them in a different manner. I understand that system is to be made uniform so that we shall have uniform reports from both the railways.
I could go on at length, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think there is much point in going over ground that will be covered when the railway officials are here. We all know that the railway business was very much better last year. I have here the figures for the first eleven months of 1955, during which period the operating revenues of the Canadian National rose from $585 million in 1954 to $623 million in 1955. Their net revenue rose from $13 million in 1954 to $52 million in 1955. We are all aware that the phrase "net revenue" refers only to operating revenue, and does not include interest and other charges, which will cause practically the whole of that $52 million to disappear. At any rate the situation is much better, and I think it is all the more reason why our committee should be put in a position to discharge more efficiently the duty which is laid upon it. It is a heavy duty, and I suggest again that efforts should be made so that we can discharge it as well as possible.
I hold in my hand the year-end review of the president of the railway. There are one or two things I saw in glancing over it. The president reports as to the new lines built during the year. There is particular reference to the Kitimat line in the far north; there is a reference to the progress being made with the Montreal hotel; and there is a reference to freight rates. We remember that during the year the matter of agreed charges was advanced. A piece of good news to a person like myself who lives in a riding which the railway traverses is that the grade crossing fund, we will remember, was increased in this house from $1 million to $6 million.

speechtext: It was increased to $5 million.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING OWNED, OPERATED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yes, $5 million. One thing I should like to mention, because I think it was of interest to all concerned, was the appointment of a very distinguished scientist in the person of Dr. Solandt to the staff of the Canadian National Railways. When the officials are here, and when the president


reports, no doubt we shall learn from him more of the background of this interesting appointment.
Before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that I feel this committee has an important job to do. I feel it cannot adequately do that job unless it gets the information well ahead of the meeting. We should also have some kind of technical assistance.
I do not think that would involve going out and hiring a lot of new and high-priced help at all. If consideration were given to it and the circumstances taken into account, and our need taken into account, it would be quite possible for officials, probably resident in Ottawa, to give us the assistance we need. At the present time what is happening is that almost imperceptibly capital charges are increasing and increasing. We know the reasons for it, but I do think it would be a good thing if we were to have a closer check on it, if we were able to have those who are most responsible give us at first hand, and not under pressure, their views regarding the matter.
I had an idea at one time myself, which I think was unsound and which I have abandoned, that it might be better for the railway to carry its own load in the matter of raising money; that it might be better for it to do all of its own financing, with necessary guarantees, of course, and not to get any further advances from the government. I have been told by those whose opinion I respect that that is not a sound idea because it would add to the cost of getting money. But I would like to have a chance, as I say, not under pressure, to talk to people whose opinion I value as to this whole situation.
Let us face the fact that the Canadian National had a difficult beginning. It was not a planned entity from beginning to end as the Canadian Pacific largely was. It began, you might say, almost as shreds and patches; it was a conglomeration of railways, nearly all of which had found difficult going themselves, and they were put together and had to be made to work as best they could. I think the progress made is very substantial, but I do feel that when this committee comes back to the House of Commons it ought to be in a better position than I consider it to be in now to report to this house and satisfy this house as to the true situation of this huge investment, which earns a gross income of as much as $600 million a year or more, and whose capital value runs into billions of dollars.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group welcome the setting up of this important and interesting committee. It

I think the place for criticism, if any, is in the committee itself. Perhaps after the report of the committee comes back to the house those who do not agree with the general finding will then have their opportunity to say something about it.
I will follow a somewhat different line from that followed by the hon. member who just took his seat. I was going to mention some of the little things, the things that are perhaps important to the general public, things which the man in the street looks at when he considers the railroads. I am aware that this committee deals with more than the railroad. We shall have the report of the Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines and what is left of the Canadian National Steamships, if I may put it that way. We shall be dealing with the auditors' reports in regard to all three.
These enterprises are, of course, of tremendous importance and magnitude. I suppose the Canadian National Railways are perhaps a $3 billion operation, or something of that nature, and they are probably almost the largest employer of labour in Canada, if not indeed the largest. Last year they had a deficit of $28 million.

Yes. I am pleased to note that the operation was more profitable in the last year; by that I mean 1955. I think every loyal Canadian would like to see the Canadian National Railways eminently successful. I know that we in this group have more reasons than one to wish it well.
This is not time to go back into the history of the Canadian National, but it has had a somewhat unfortunate history. In my opinion it has never had a chance; it has been a sort of overcapitalized conglomeration of unprofitable ventures. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) mentioned that sort of thing the other day when he was talking about the railroad that is being built to bring out the Labrador iron ore. He said that the railroad was being built and equipped to serve that particular function, but if or when the reason for its being disappeared, then he presumed the Canadian National would be asked to take it over to join a number of other lines of the same sort.
Now, sir, the financial structure of the Canadian National Railways has been ameliorated, of course, by the government action of some years ago. So far as I am concerned that, and matters of a similar nature, are 67509-117
Committee on Railways and Shipping matters for the experts, the accountants and the financiers. My interest, as I said at the beginning, just for the moment at least, is in the man on the street, the consumer of the service that is provided.
We are also vitally interested in the welfare of the vast army of Canadian National employees. I think it is a matter of great importance that this road, which is a national road and the property of us all, should stand high in the regard of the public and of the employees who work in its service. I say this particularly because it is nationally owned. Its function and the criterion by which it must be judged is of course the service it provides to the public, and I am not convinced that simply to say it must make a profit is to be realistic.
Everybody knows there have been occasions this year when heavy snow and intense cold brought about a condition which road men would call "tough railroading", and I know that services have been pretty freely withdrawn in certain districts of Saskatchewan on that account. There has also been the fact that grain has not been able to move freely because there is nowhere it may be moved and that, too, is a consideration. I simply want to draw to the attention of the house the fact that I think there are times when it is justified to maintain public service even if in fact that public service does not show a profit in black upon the balance sheet. The popularity of the road depends on the quality of the service.
What are matters of concern to the average user of the railroads? I suppose from a business point of view one*nust first mention freight rates. I do not think this is the time to go into a discussion of that sort of thing. As far as passengers are concerned, I think the speed and comfort of the service are essential. We are also concerned with the working conditions and the pay of the people who work on the road. On working conditions, pay and pension arrangements, and that sort of thing, morale largely depends.
I think morale is particularly important in this particular operation. Morale is certainly going to have an effect on whether or not the Canadian National Railways is considered as a first-class operation. We have to face the fact that the Canadian National Railways is pitted against efficient and strenuous rivalry from the Canadian Pacific Railway. We have to meet that competition, and in this matter I think the morale of the workers is particularly important.
There are two matters I want to mention in this connection. These may look like small matters, but I think they are important. What do we hear from the man in the street, the
1842	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping man who travels on the cars? What do we hear when we hear these railroads compared? One might be surprised to know that people regard the possession of domed observation cars by the Canadian Pacific as an important advantage, and the fact that the Canadian National has no domed cars is a matter of importance to them at least. I simply draw this to your attention.
Another matter of importance is speed. As I have stated before I do not see why in this vast country, with travel involving a large number of miles, the Canadian National has to take two hours longer than the Canadian Pacific in reaching Vancouver. It has been explained to me that the Canadian National gets to Winnipeg faster than its rival; we have heard that story before. Many hon. members will recall what Mr. Gordon has described as the greatest railway myth of all time, when it used to be asserted that at any time the Canadian National could spurt up a bit and improve its speed by ten hours on the transcontinental trip and thereby beat the Canadian Pacific into Vancouver or Montreal by that amount of time. He described that as the greatest myth in railroad history, and he may be right.
However, I would draw to his attention and to the attention of the house that when one or both roads decided to step up their time they decided suddenly it was quite possible to speed up by some ten hours, and both roads were able to do that.
One point which has been drawn to my attention two or three times is this. Why in the world when it decided to increase its speed, did the Canadian National not increase its speed to the same extent the other railroad did? What is an hour's time in travelling across this vast continent? Those are little things, but they are important.
Before I started this discussion of detail I was talking about morale, and there are examples of the little things that build morale. Belonging to an effective organization, a crack organization, must have the effect of building morale, whereas belonging to an organization which is less than first class must have the opposite effect.
At this time I should like to pay tribute and extend a word of congratulation to the Canadian National Railways on the improvement in its dining car facilities. While I take no credit whatever for the change in the management's opinion in that regard, the fact remains that for five or six years I have suggested that something be done about dining car rates in this country. As far as I am concerned the national railroad should have only one object in view, and that is to serve the public, to serve the greatest number of the public.
[Mr. Knight.l

A few years ago the situation was such that only a small percentage of the travelling public in Canada was able to buy meals on the train; it was not financially possible for the general public to make use of the dining facilities on trains. It used to make one's heard bleed to see a mother with three or four young children travelling thousands of miles, involving several days and nights on the train. Upon entering the dining car one frequently saw such a woman glancing at the menu, shake her head slowly and then order a glass of milk or something for the children and not eating anything herself. I have seen this myself. Everyone is familiar with the constant cry of travellers, "When do we stop for ten minutes so we can get off and get something to eat"? I think that has been the experience everywhere.
We in Canada compare rather unfavourably with certain European countries in this regard. I am not suggesting that we should adopt the afternoon tea habit, but if you have ever travelled from London to Edinburgh or from Liverpool to London you will have observed that everybody on the train has afternoon tea. My idea of the function of a dining car service, particularly in this great country where people would eat two or three meals a day if they could afford to do so, is to provide a service that will be within the means of all the travelling passengers. I am not talking about the first-class coaches, nor do I refer particularly to the tourist coaches. I am talking about the people who travel on what we call the day coaches. I think there has been a great improvement in this regard, and I should like to congratulate the management for this.
I know there are some people who do not like the present arrangement; they dislike crowds and demand privacy and all that sort of thing. Most of the trains now have arrangements for that. The people who desire a meal involving privacy and better service can obtain it at a somewhat higher price. The condition I have long hoped for and spoken about, wherein everyone can get something to eat at a reasonable price even if it is only a light lunch, a hot dog or a cup of coffee, has come about, and people now do not have to be hungry while travelling.
I have been discussing working conditions, and I cannot refrain from mentioning the question of C.N.R. pensions. I know that in doing this I am infringing upon the field of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has made this one of his many causes on behalf of the underprivileged. This is a great organization in which we have not only a moral but a financial interest, and we think it should be more generous with

those people who have served it in the past but who now find themselves caught in the squeeze of the high cost of living. The knowledge that there is a good pension system is a morale builder in any organization.
There are one or two local matters with which we in the west are concerned. I have already mentioned the fact that service has been eliminated or lessened on certain branch lines, particularly in northern Saskatchewan. I have said already that I do not think profit is the only thing that should be taken into account. Service should be maintained, and certainly during the type of winter we have had this year it was not the time to carry out an economy of that sort.
Then I should like to refer also to the box car shortage, and in doing this I assure you I am not going to reopen the debate on wheat. The responsibility for the box car shortage has been bandied back and forth on the government side of the house until we really do not know where the responsibility lies. However, I note from a reply given to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as reported on page 1606 of Hansard of February 27, that the Canadian National Railways has a large number of box cars on order. The term "large" is comparative. Who am I to say what is a large number of box cars for an institution like the Canadian National Railways? But I am glad to see that at least some box cars are on order.
One thing that has troubled the farmer in the west is that he hears about space being available in certain elevators but he finds there are no box cars to permit him to deliver his grain there, so he could get at least some money for it. I draw this fact to the attention of the railway. I take it that the management know what they are doing; I take it that they have taken into consideration the present shortage in placing their orders, and I am glad to see that some of the new box cars have been delivered and are being put into service.
There is another question about box cars, and that is the number which are perambulating around the United States. I do not know whether this situation is normal, but if hon. members will look at page 1826 of Hansard of March 5 they will see where the minister made a reply to the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson) indicating the number of box cars at present on United States lines. Many people have the feeling that these box cars are down there longer than is necessary, and I suppose their wish is that the cars were available here rather than being kept in the United States for so long.
I should like to indicate my pleasure at the success last year of the Hudson Bay railroad.

The wheat shipments established a record, and I wish there had also been a record established in the case of goods being shipped in. I note that in 1954 there were 36 ships at Churchill and 12,485,000 bushels of grain were shipped to northern Europe. Those shipments exceeded the 1953 figure by five ships and 1,700,000 bushels. As far as the port itself was concerned the turnaround time was reduced to an average of 3-6 days as compared with 5 [DOT] 6 days for the year previous.
The people in the northern part of my province are tremendously interested in this operation. They look upon it as being something of their own. They have always had an interest in this port railroad, which I think can be explained by the feeling that prairie people have for water. You may be interested to know that on a Sunday afternoon you can drive along our rather sluggish and muddy South Saskatchewan-I hope I will not get into trouble by saying that- in my city and see hundreds and hundreds of cars parked on the river bank with the people just watching the water run over the dam. It is a prairie habit to go to the nearest water and this habit is well founded in history. We all remember the drought in the dry years of 1930-37.
Perhaps that is one reason we are interested in our port. We feel that after all we are not so far from the sea, and in the case of some of us it brings us that much closer to the country of our origin. We have a pride in that port and we want it to succeed. We congratulate everybody concerned, the government, the railroad and everyone else upon bringing about the realization of an ambition to get this operation on its feet. If in the next year there is an increase in proportion to the increase of last year, we feel that we will have realized at least the first step in our ambition.
There are many other problems connected with the railroads but I am not competent nor have I the time to discuss them at the moment. There is the matter of truck competition, or the co-ordination of railroads with the trucks. There is the matter of a national board to control transportation. There is also the question of level crossing elimination and all the rest. We welcome the setting up of this committee, and shall look forward with interest to its discussions.

If I had not heard anybody comment "Hear, hear", as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did, when I made that remark, maybe I would have been wrong; but he is happy in the thought that Canada is gradually being socialized and he sees here an opportunity to carry on more of the socialism despite the fact that the members of the government, or the members of the Liberal party itself, so frequently say they are the free enterprise party in this country.
Why do I suggest that socialism is creeping into Canadian life more and more? We have for instance, the fact that when the railways first went bankrupt, the Canadian National Railway Company was formed under the government to operate those railways, and for a good purpose; for when free enterprise fails to offer a means for carrying on the services within the country, I feel it is up to the government to provide the people the facilities they require.
However, from that point on we had the gradual development of the Trans-Canada Air Lines, which today will not harbour any competition. As Canadian taxpayers we are being denied the right to cheaper transportation which Canadian Pacific Air Lines would offer us across the pole to Europe. I know this matter is perhaps not one that would concern so many people, because there will not be many people using the facilities to go to Europe from this country. However, it is a matter of some concern when one also realizes that not so many months ago Pacific Western Airlines was denied a service across Canada in direct competition with Trans-Canada Air Lines because Trans-Canada could not stand the competition. They knew that it would mean cheaper fares for the people in Canada who wanted to travel by air.
We have here the creeping paralysis of socialism in regard to such a company as Canadian Pacific Air Lines. When United States travellers or any other travellers who want to go to Europe are denied the same fares as would be available if they went by
Committee on Railways and Shipping another air line, then I would say that other company is going to get the business. That is exactly what is happening. People who want to use air services from Winnipeg, such as the Scandinavian Air Service, are denied that also. There is no getting around it. We have here a monopoly which cannot and will not harbour any competition; and that is wrong in principle. If the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines, Canadian National Railways and the steamship service are to be continued in their present form, then these organizations should be prepared to stand up to any kind of competition.
We are told that the Canadian National Railways are losing money because of the great big truck transport lines, and that the railway is going to inaugurate a piggy-back service to compete with the truckers with the idea of getting rid of the truck competition through having a lower rate for the railway service. If you get rid of the trucking industry what will you have? You will have more socialization, and you will have put a certain number of people out of business.
The setting up of the committee will give us the opportunity to find out how many truckers have been put out of business, and I hoPe we will not be denied that privilege. We will be denied it unless we are. able to call witnesses from the trucking firms. I think we should have the privilege of calling witnesses from Canadian Pacific Air Lines, Pacific Western Airlines, the various trucking organizations and hotel companies who will be competing with the new palace that is being built in Montreal. I think we should have the officials before us in order to investigate these matters. We should have the privilege of asking these witnesses to come before us so they can discuss their problems with us so far as competition is concerned, and how they are gradually being forced out of business because these government-owned organizations are carrying on in this fashion.
I also feel that the setting up of the committee will give us the opportunity to look into the labour problem again. Here I should like to compliment the railway officials for coming to an agreement with the brotherhoods with respect to the hiring of men for work done under contract, as in the case of the Welch company. I understand that matter has been amicably settled. That is a good, sound practice. But these are the things we find taking place, and we must guard against this creeping paralysis of socialism. We must protect the interests of the taxpayers and guard against the setting up of various industries by Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the motion to set up a sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government to consider the accounts and estimates and bills relating thereto.
To begin with, I should like to say a few words of congratulation to our railways for the additional service they have provided by way of making it more comfortable for people wishing to travel from coast to coast. However, I do not think we should limit our consideration of comfort only to the rolling stock and motive power. I believe we should go a little beyond that. It is a great thing that we have fine hotels, but somewhere between the rolling stock and the hotels some consideration should be given to the railway stations and the methods of travelling to one's home from the station or vice versa.
I am not going to say anything about the Kingston station this time. All I can say is that it is just that much worse by being one year older. However, for a few moments I should like to discuss the matter of issuing monopolistic franchises to certain taxi companies throughout the country with respect to service at various stations. It is true that the

franchises are granted by tender, and that the highest bidder is the one who receives the franchise. I might say at our local station in Kingston it is given, by tender, to a highly reputable taxi company. They received the franchise, and as far as they are concerned they are doing a good job. But taking the matter beyond that point, may I say this. Complaints have been made to me, and on taking them up with the officials I have been told that it is the uniform thing to do, that they must continue to use this franchise method of awarding contracts to taxi companies to deliver people from the station to their homes or wherever they wish to go.
This system may be all right in a large city where there is a problem in connection with the control of traffic outside the station as well as on the station or railway property. But in a city of the size of Kingston people normally have become accustomed to having personalized taxi service, where you become a customer of a taxi company or of an individual operating one or two taxis. He will come and pick you up and take you to the station, and will also be there to meet you to take you to your home from the station.
The idea of the franchise may be all right, as I have said, in a large city; but in a small city I do not agree with that idea. In a place like Kingston, having regard to the location of the station area itself, it assists the railway officials in policing a station area by having only one taxi service calling for people. But if a passenger on a train wishes to have his own taxi come and pick him up, it is necessary for him to walk a city block, carry his luggage, get his own taxi and make arrangements for it to be there rather than taking a taxi which has the franchise.
I should just like to bring this thought to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, and indicate a direction of inquiry to anybody on the committee who might wish to go into the matter. Because you wish to travel by rail and buy a ticket, I cannot see why the railway service which provides your rail transportation should therefore, by their franchise, award the taxi service^-and I say quite properly "award" it-by tender and direct how you should go to your home. I feel that it should be left to private enterprise. I cannot see why in Kingston or in cities of that size it cannot be left to private enterprise to handle and not be handled by franchise, when there is little reason other than that it is usual in larger cities to do so.

I believe that was in 1944.
Mr. King laid down the government's postwar civil aviation policy. I remember in particular the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking in that debate and referring to some of the unfortunate experiences we had had in this country in connection with the building of our railroads. He referred to the large number of railroads which had been built and the financial problems and problems of capitalization which developed and which led to the eventual necessity of forming the Canadian National Railways to take over a number of bankrupt lines.
I do not think I would be unfair to the Minister of Trade and Commerce if I said that in his speech in 1944 he made it clear that the government did not wish to see that story repeated in the field of aviation. The point was made at that time, with which we agreed and with which we still agree, that because of the nature of aviation, because of the greater attention that has to be paid to the safety factor, because of the greater cost involved in building air lines, because of the greater cost to the public treasury involved in providing aids to air navigation and so on, considerations which had been learned out of the experience with the railroads were even more important so far as civil aviation was concerned.
As the minister will recall, we gave full support to the government's policy as laid down in 1944. That has been done in many jurisdictions where pensions of retired employees have been increased. I emphasize that because one of the points the minister and his predecessor have tried to make is that the pension these men are now receiving is in pursuance of the contractual arrangement that existed between the railway and the workers. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, since these alleged contractual arrangements were entered into, conditions have changed. The cost of living has gone up, the standard of living has gone up, the productivity of the nation and of a railway such as the Canadian National has increased, and it seems to me that Canadian National Railways as a good employer has a moral obligation to these retired employees.
I urge it upon the minister as strongly as I can that he should give consideration to this matter. After all, we are impressed with the way in which the minister has taken hold of his department. He has now been with us for a couple of years or more and is no longer a novice. He no longer has to do only the things that were done by his


predecessor. He is a full-fledged minister now, and I suggest it is time that he himself took a personal look as a human being at this problem and came up with an answer to it. If he would like to do so on some occasion we could have a discussion as to ways and means whereby this matter might be dealt with, but the first concern, of course, is that there be a will to deal with it, and to us it is a matter of real regret that as yet neither the minister nor the management of the railways have shown any real concern for the position of these retired employees.
Let the minister not come back and say that the plan so far as those who are working is concerned is better than it was. That is true. It has been improved immeasurably, but by and large that does not help men retired when the pensions that they received were smaller. It does not help at all those who get only $25 a month. I know the arguments about the difference between the contributory and the non-contributory plans, between service pensions and the pensions of other categories, but I submit that whatever argument may be made about the contractual arrangement the Canadian Pacific Railway has given at least a partial answer to that because, as I say, that railway has made this slight improvement.
I repeat what the Canadian Pacific has done. It has provided that any retired employee, whose pension arising out of his contractual arrangement is less than $60 a month, will have that pension increased to the figure of $60 a month at least until such time as that employee reaches the age of 70. As I say, there are some other details about it that we may have to discuss in the house later this session, but for the moment I simply make the point that surely the Canadian National should be able to do just as well as the Canadian Pacific with regard to its retired employees.
I am happy, Mr. Speaker, to have included in my remarks today a few words of pride and commendation, of pride in these crown corporations and commendation for what the government has done. I am happy to have included an endorsation of the government's policy with regard to civil aviation. But the other side of the coin is that we feel resentful and annoyed over the way in which consideration of this important matter has been put off and off. I hope that the present Minister of Transport, as a human being, will give it serious consideration and will do something very soon to raise the pensions of retired C.N.R. employees, particularly those whose pensions are in the lower and the middle brackets.

Mr: A. M. Nicholson (Mackenzie):	Mr. Speaker, before the main motion is decided I should like to make a few remarks. I abbreviated my remarks the other evening to oblige the Minister of Finance in the hope that we might reach a decision before six o'clock. But since that was not possible, and there are a number of hon. members present who were not present on Friday, I should like to review very briefly this case, which, as I said the other day, is the first contested case which has reached us this session.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), mentioned, this case involves a Hungarian couple who were married some 29 years ago. There is one 14-year-old daughter involved. If this

divorce is granted the father will be relieved of his responsibility to support his wife and daughter.
Apparently at one stage the petitioner signed some document that appears to be a mortgage of about $7,000, which was to be paid in monthly instalments of $100 provided that his wife left. That is not too clearly established. As my colleague mentioned, these people are not able to speak English too well. It appears that there was some difficulty in understanding the questions, and the answers were not always quite to the point. The lawyer representing the respondent tried to establish the fact that these payments of $100 a month were made on the condition that the wife leave the domicile. Eventually she did leave and the payments of $100 a month went through for some 10 months. Then the petitioner's lawyer advised his client against continuing those payments, and apparently a letter was written suggesting that if the respondent returned she and the daughter would be permitted to come home. The petitioner was examined by the counsel for the respondent as follows:
Q. You refer to a housekeeper. Is it a male or female housekeeper?
A. Well, it is female housekeeper.
Q. You describe her as a housekeeper?
A. She work for me with money. I paid her $50 a month.
Q. Have you any receipts for that?
A. Me not need any receipt for that.
Q. Then you cannot prove or establish that you did pay any money at all?
A. Well, sure. Well, she was prove it. I not call anybody when I pay her.
Q. No. You had no witnesses and no evidence that you pay her?
A. I told the truth.
There was not any proof that this housekeeper was paid. Then, there were some questions about the living quarters. The man was asked about his house. He said there were three rooms and a kitchen. After a little while it turned out to be four rooms and a kitchen. According to the evidence, the petitioner slept in the dining room on a couch and his housekeeper had a bedroom which could not be entered except through the dining room. The petitioner's clothes were kept in this bedroom. That was the evidence submitted. The counsel for the respondent went on to say:
I do not want to elaborate on this point but the fact remains there is a woman living in the same flat for some reason.
He went on to point out that this is something which should be noted by Their Honours the senators. The chairman, Senator Ross-I may say that I had very happy associations with Senator Ross when he was a member of the House of Commons; he sat on

a different side of the house and we differed in our opinions at times-said:
I do not think the inquiries you have been following are very material because the petitioner is not on trial here. The question is not whether or not he committed adultery. The question is whether or not the respondent committed adultery.
Counsel went on to say:
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I thought it was a valid defence on the part of the party who may have committed adultery-who is alleged to have committed adultery, if the man who is alleging it, is himself or is, as he suggests, living with another woman. I merely wanted to bring that forward.
The respondent went on to say that she had three more witnesses, and then counsel for the petitioner took exception and said:
But you should have somebody to testify here.
Here is a woman who is working for $21 a week washing dishes. It was not possible for her to bring a lot of witnesses to Ottawa to defend herself. Then Senator Ross said:
I probably went too far. If the petitioner has been guilty of misconduct, it is a discretionary matter for us to refuse the divorce. Perhaps I went too far in my statement.
Later on the counsel for the petitioner, in reviewing the payments of $100 a month, mentioned what I mentioned previously, namely, that payments were going forward to this woman who was living in Ontario. He said:
And, he stopped making the payments in the first place according to my advice because the wife cannot be given anything in the form of a mortgage under the laws of Quebec.
Therefore, these payments were discontinued. Then, counsel for the respondent pointed out:
The idea was that the man insisted she leave, at least that is the idea the contestant will try to establish. It was made when the man tried to insist that she leave the premises.
She did leave. Counsel for the respondent says, at page 16:
He says it is to keep his wife and I will try to prove it is just the opposite conclusion that instead it gave me the conclusion he was willing to offer his wife $100 a month provided his wife was willing to move out. You do not keep the wife in the home by consecutive monthly payments of $100. The point is, as you so very aptly put it, is for the courts to decide on any property issue. It is just I wanted to challenge the suggestion put forward by the witness.
Then, the investigators gave evidence, and as usual there is a good deal of contradictory evidence given by them. I suggest that hon. members have a look at it. When the respondent was being questioned, the counsel for the petitioner was a bit annoyed. At page 22 of the evidence he is reported as' saying:
What has it got to do with this hearing supposing her husband did beat her? The proper thing to do 
would have been to take a separation action before the court in Montreal.
There was some question about the beating of the petitioner and the petitioner's counsel challenged it. On page 29 the counsel for the petitioner said:
Q. You heard your wife state you beat her?
A. I never beat her in my life only when she tried to come back when you send her a letter to come.
Later on when being examined by the counsel for the respondent, at page 30, he admitted:
I thump her on that time.
The questioning continued on page 31 as follows:
Q. What did you say?
A. Nothing. I just told her go out from my house.
Q. Was that the time you hit her?
A. Yes, I hit her.
Although at one point he stated very definitely that he never beat his wife in his life, after a little mature thought he did admit that he had beaten her.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to establish that either of these two parties is a saint. I do not think we have black and white in these cases. However, I do not think we are justified on the basis of the evidence before us in relieving the husband of the financial responsibility to care for his 14-year-old daughter and his wife. If the respondent had been seeking a divorce I think there would have been no question about its going through.
It seems to me this case is very similar to the one we handled last year, No. 490, which passed at this stage and after being reviewed by the committee on miscellaneous private bills it was agreed to report the preamble thereof, not proven, on the ground that the committee was not satisfied that the petitioner was worthy of having his petition granted. I should think that would be the treatment this house should give to this petition in connection with Bill No. 158.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 149, to amend the Financial Administration Act.
Financial Administration Act He said: This bill, now at the second reading stage, embodies an amendment to chapter 116 of Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, entitled "Financial Administration Act". Section 33 of that chapter provides:
Every payment pursuant to an appropriation .	.	. shall be made under the direction andcontrol of the comptroller by cheque drawn on the account of the Receiver General or other instrument, .	.	.
The present amendment, while adding section 33a to section 33 already embodied in the act, provides that negotiable instruments referred to in such section shall from now on be printed in both official languages, and it covers all segments of every department and of any crown corporation as defined in section 76 (1) (c).
I have no doubt that the change suggested under the present bill will meet the wishes of the wide majority of the members of the house and prove at least acceptable to the others. In point of fact, the spirit, if not the letter, of the constitution recognizes that this is a bilingual country, and every day we hear outstanding English Canadians uphold that point of view. Common sense also bears out that claim. As a matter of fact, if the constitution recognized, to either of the great races it wanted to bring closer, the right of preserving its language, it certainly put at its disposal the right of using the written language as well as the spoken language. One of the best means of recognizing publicly that right to use the written language is by imparting to it an official place on the bills which pass steadily under the eyes of Canadian citizens-cheques and other similar instruments.
It should be emphasized that there are in Canada, outside Quebec, about one million loyal French Canadian subjects who are entitled to that recognition and who are at home everywhere in Canada, in British Columbia as well as in Nova Scotia, just as English Canadians are at home in Quebec as everywhere else in Canada. For instance, have you pondered over the fact that there are more French Canadians outside Quebec than the aggregate population of any of the three prairie provinces, almost as many as in British Columbia alone, or in the three maritime provinces combined? Such a group is entitled, for that matter, to some consideration and to an official recognition of its rights. Who would dare submit such a racial element makes up a class of citizens less commendable than the others? Why then treat them with less care and on an inferior basis?
Besides, what we are asking in this bill is directed only to the federal administration. Nobody has ever thought of asking provincial
1860	HOUSE OF
Financial Administration Act administrations to go so far, and I know of none other than the province of Quebec, which in that field does not rest content with following the letter of the constitution but goes far beyond the limit to be reached in abiding by its spirit. The proposition has nothing to do with the private affairs of our people and will never prevent the latter from giving their exchange media the linguistic character of their choice.
A spirit of tolerance and the obvious desire for good understanding which is found in the English Canadian element in this house make up another factor that enables us to hope for the passing of this measure. Of course, there are some snags here and there in some provinces, but I ascribe that situation much more to a lack of information than to intolerance or bad feeling.
In 1952, the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Abbott, promised to a delegation of the French Life Council that as soon as circumstances should warrant it all cheques would be bilingual right across Canada. About the same time, the present and genial Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) stated at a public meeting in Windsor that nothing prevented the issuance of bilingual cheques for Canada as a whole, at least in regard to family allowances.
As far as the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is concerned, for whom I have great respect, he wrote on November 8, 1954, in answer to a resolution the French Life Council had sent to him about the bilingual cheques issue:
Surely you will agree with me about the swift extension of bilingualism to other parts of the country now going on. I do not have to tell you that is being made with my full support, and, furthermore, it took place without bringing up undesirable controversies. I am positive you will hope with me that the trend will be maintained.
I also hope he did not change his mind and that the present bill will provide the minister with an excellent opportunity to carry out his wishes, the more so since he no doubt needs the warm support of the French element in this country, since one points to him as the potential successor to the Prime Minister at the head of the Liberal party. However, it is my ardent wish-and I trust, sir, you appreciate how sincere I am- that the problem of this succession will not crop up before quite a number of years.
Finally, we have two precedents on which I might rest to ask for bilingual cheques: money and postage stamps.
In 1934, the Conservative party, which was then at the helm of this country, made a praiseworthy gesture when giving us French money and English money. In 1936 the 

Liberal government which succeeded them made that piece of legislation still better by giving to the present-day money its final and perfectly bilingual character. Which of those great parties would accept today the disowning of its past and take away from that gesture made years ago its character of magnanimity through refusing to take one more step in the fine direction to which they then turned? With a general election fast approaching, such a stand is certainly untimely.
(Translation) ;
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to conclude my remarks with a few words in French.
In certain quarters, people contend that there is a fundamental difference between money and cheques or other similar instruments, that money has a permanent character while a cheque's useful life is quite short. May I say in the first place while those cheques are undoubtedly short-lived we keep seeing them continually, replaced as they are by others, and they are constantly in circulation. Because of that uninterrupted circulation, cheques take on the same character of permanency as currency itself. Incidentally, the so-called permanent character of paper money is only apparent, for $1 and $2 bills have to be printed every nine or ten months.
Besides, it is known that as a consequence of the development of financial institutions, and of improved methods of doing business, about 80 per cent of the business carried on by the public at large is done by means of cheques. Those modern means of exchange have therefore acquired a great importance.
I readily admit that, according to the letter of the Canadian constitution, there is no actual obligation to use bilingual wording on cheques any more than on paper money or on coins; on the other hand, it can also be said that there is nothing to prevent it.
It is the common sense of the house and the evident desire of hon. members for fairness, as well as the spirit of the constitution, which brought about the acts of 1934 and 1936, to which I referred a moment ago and which legalized the bilingual wording on money. It is to that same common sense and that same desire of the house for fairness- whose members are no longer the same, but they are no less brilliant and are surely as well intentioned as their predecessors-that I now appeal today in favour of a bilingual wording on cheques and other instruments of exchange.
I also appeal to the tolerance and earnest desire for good understanding which seem to be shared by all members of this house.

I do not see why anyone should oppose this legislation, which would merely do justice to a racial element representing one third of the population of this country, especially one whose ancestors were the very ones who opened Canada to civilization, were its first settlers and who valiantly fought for its defence. After the conquest, they displayed the same enthusiasm, the same courage and the same loyalty toward the country's new rulers as they had shown in their attempt to defend it against them. Those who today live in this beautiful country, whatever their racial origin, are indebted to the French Canadian element for the advantage of being at home here in Canada, and for having escaped absorption by the great republic to the south.
In sessional paper No. 225, dated June 15, 1955, tabled in answer to a question I had put on the order paper, I was told that the St. Lawrence seaway authority issues bilingual cheques all over Canada. With a few exceptions, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does the same thing.
I compare those two cases with those of bilingual postage stamps and money, and I ask the following question: has any Canadian suffered from that new situation? Has he been deprived of any of his rights or privileges due to the fact that the two official languages appear simultaneously on the bills of exchange I have just mentioned?
If an hon. member could rise in this house and describe a single case of this type, I would be prepared to withdraw my bill at once.
Far from this being the case, Mr. Speaker, many of the most cultured, learned and prominent people, of whatever racial origin, point out everywhere, in Canada and abroad, the advantages of cultural and racial duality. Now then, the basic vehicle of any culture, and the primary characteristic of any race, is first and foremost the language, spoken and written. Why then should written language in Canada be denied all possible chances of demonstrating to the world at large the reality of this highly praised duality?
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help quoting briefly from an article which appeared on June 17, 1955 in Le Soleil of Quebec city under the signature of Gerard Morin. I quote:
It seems inconceivable that, in the twentieth century, one should still have to fight in Canada for a matter as simple as bilingual wording on cheques issued by the federal government.
I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that this government, being well disposed, will not
Financial Administration Act miss this opportunity to remedy a situation which even its friends consider inconceivable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five
o'clock I had just referred to the fact that, resulting from discussions in this house, a change has been made in connection with the company to which I made reference, namely, the Welch Company, that has been a most beneficial one, and one that is deeply appreciated by the employees of the Canadian National Railways.
I wish to refer for a moment to Trans-Canada Air Lines, having regard particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He went all out this afternoon and stated that anyone who criticized the operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines was trying to scuttle that corporation. It is not a question of wanting to scuttle the corporation at all. What we of the Progressive Conservative party believe is that the time has come for active competition by private enterprise to be permitted in the operation of air lines. Indeed, we are fortified in our view in that regard by the words of the Prime Minister in a speech made before the air industries and transport association in November, 1953, which were quoted earlier this afternoon. During the period when the Canadian Pacific Air Lines' application to operate a freight service was being considered the Prime Minister said in part, it:-and I merely refer to one or two portions-
. . . the demands for the services of commercial aircraft should increase to such an extent that increasing competition will be both desirable and beneficial . . .
He also went on to say that in the long run he was not in favour of the perpetuation of monopoly conditions. Well, there can be no justification today for the continuation of that monopoly condition under which Trans-Canada Air Lines operate. I mention in particular the operation of freight transport. The failure to grant a licence to Canadian Pacific Air Lines to operate freight services is holding back to a very considerable degree development in the western provinces and generally throughout those areas of Canada which
Committee on Railways and Shipping would be served by the granting of such a licence. I cannot understand the dog-in-the-manger attitude of Trans-Canada Air Lines in continuing, now that it is perfectly established, an attitude antipathetic to competition. There is no reason why competition should not be permitted. It has been denied with regard to freight; it has also been denied to one air line company which desired to operate a passenger transportation service. The time has come to take the hobbles off air development in Canada, to remove the shackles of an outgrown policy that denies competition, and to give Canadians those benefits that competitive enterprise will assure.
In its passenger transportation Trans-Canada Air Lines have provided a high degree of safety, and for that they are worthy of commendation. No one who user the airways to the extent that some of us do can deny that in too many instances the service bears a resemblance to that expected from monopoly, bureaucratic enterprise. If competition were allowed, the service and the relationship which should exist between the transportation organization and the travelling public would be very greatly improved.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that when we take a stand in favour of competition we are out to destroy Trans-Canada Air Lines. Nothing of the sort is contemplated. But surely when a public body has arrived at the point where its service year by year operates almost to the extent of its physical limitations the time has come for active competition.
We in the Conservative party are not opposed to public enterprise as such. There are certain types of industries in the form of public monopolies that can be operated most efficiently as public enterprises; but our experience in Saskatchewan has been this. However desirable the purpose in mind may be, government in competitive business does not succeed. We have had various lines of business in Saskatchewan-I am not going into that this evening-but they did not pay taxes. They did not pay interest on their investment, and yet they found it necessary to close down. They could not compete against private industry allegedly charging exorbitant profits, according to the proponents of the government in that province, and yet the government-operated enterprises were so inefficiently operated that they were unable to return a profit.
When one speaks of development, the government of that province had very desirable aims. They thought they could abolish the lessons of arithmetic and change the experiences of human nature that history

Yes. I am not only with you in what I am going to deal with, I was ahead of you in bringing it up. I brought it up as far back as 1946 and I pointed out the injustice that was being done to Canadian National Railways employees who were retired on a basic pension of only $25 a month. That basic pension is today in equivalent purchasing power something like $9 or $10 at the time it was brought into effect. If there


is one thing that is necessary to raise the standard of Canadian National Railways service it is that the morale of the employees be maintained at the highest possible level. The morale of Canadian National Railways employees today in most cases is lower than it has been at any time in my experience because the employees feel they are not receiving the consideration they deserve.
One of the things which would assist would be the removal of the present low level of the basic pension. It should be increased at least to $40 a month. That would not be very costly. I am speaking from memory but I believe that pensions today cost approximately 2-7 per cent of the total amount taken in by the Canadian National Railways. The increase in question would be infinitesimal having regard to the total amount of business done and would raise beyond words of description the morale of the employees of the railway company.
There is another thing which could be done. The rules regarding pensions were in effect for many years unchanged. Finally there were reformed or revised rules established within the last three or four years but there are many employees who should be entitled to consideration who find themselves in the paradoxical position of having expected that their disability in connection with the pensions under the regulation would be removed in the revision, only to find they have not been. I suggest to the minister that if he would let it be known to the Canadian National Railways employees across Canada that this committee, which is being set up, would set aside from among it's membership a subcommittee to give consideration to the pension regulations in order to remove the anomalies that exist and the injustices that are taking place, he would have gone a long way towards restoring and increasing the morale of these employees.
As a matter of fact the regulations with regard to the continuity of employment are totally at variance with reality. There are many cases of individual employees who should be entitled to longer periods of pension qualification but who are denied the total period they have served because of certain inequities which have crept into the regulations. Another point is that if an employee is out of work and goes on unemployment insurance there is a break in his employment. The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) has referred to these injustices over and over again. There is no reason at all why the pension regulations should not be changed in order to provide that, during a period when a railway employee is receiving

Committee on Railways and Shipping
unemployment insurance, this period should count in his pension qualification period. This has frequently been the contention of the hon. member for Perth. It is something which represents a real demand on the part of the railway employees of this country.
In summarizing I simply say this. The time has come and it is long overdue when the basic pension of Canadian National Railways employees should be increased. Secondly, I join with my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in suggesting to the minister that the Canadian Pacific Railway, a private corporation, having seen fit to make changes such as have been referred to by him in detail, there is no justification for the railway of the people of Canada doing less than its competitor is doing. I also suggest that if the Canadian National Railways is to secure its fair and proper share of the competitive dollar in this country it should certainly do a lot more than it is doing to elevate the standard of its trans-Canada train. It is a fine train but it can be improved a great deal more in order to meet the competition provided by the Canadian Pacific Railway and its trans-Canada train. Too frequently individuals having no preference one for the other take the Canadian Pacific Railway train in cases where the Canadian National Railways train would ordinarily be taken.
Now we pass on to another matter which has to do with the transportation of goods and merchandise. Mention has already been made of the box car situation.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) blandly brushes this aside, saying, there are lots of cars; everything is fine. Within the last week, on February 28, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, a non-political organization, came to this conclusion, as reported in a recent press dispatch:
Persistent shortages of box cars for movement of grain from the prairies have made deep cuts into the current income of many western farmers.
It then goes on to deal with the situation as it exists. I would point out that the manner in which box car distribution has been made on the prairies would seem to indicate that those in authority on the Canadian National Railways have little regard to the needs of the western provinces. It may be that box car traffic hauling other than wheat is more remunerative, but there can be no justification for the cavalier disregard that has been shown to the requirements of the western provinces and the farmers who inhabit those provinces.
The records show that in a period of five months from the first of August until the 67509-118
first of February on the prairies there were some 32,000 less cars hauling wheat than in the previous year. There has been a near collapse of freight transportation for wheat on the prairies and in large measure this is responsible for the financial condition which exists today. It cannot be offered as an excuse that there was no place to which to haul the grain, because there was vacant storage available running well up to 100 million bushels.
These are one or two matters that I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister. I recapitulate. In so far as railway pensions are concerned, what possible reason can be given to deny the almost universal desire on the part of railway employees to have a reconsideration of the rules governing the payment of their pensions and for the removal of injustices, inequities and anomalies which have crept into the administration of these regulations, as they creep into the administration of all regulations when tested in the light of experience?
If that were given there would be a changed attitude. If the minister would travel incognito across the country on the trains of the Canadian National Railways and ask the employees what they think of the administration as they see it today he would receive a reaction of depressed morale which would be a revelation to him. What I am trying to place before the house at this time is that that state of mind on the part of the railway employees is not conducive to expansion or to securing the largest possible share of the competitive freight dollar.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me to be most fortunate that the debate on this resolution follows the debate of yesterday on the development and decentralization of industry in which transportation plays such a vital role. In his excellent contribution to yesterday's debate my friend and colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Fraser), showed that the economic life and welfare of our province is completely dependent upon our means of transportation. As the main transportation system of Newfoundland is government-owned, I feel I should intervene in this debate to carry on where my hon. friend left off yesterday and develop this theme a little more fully.
It is evident that we must plan now for the future. Time flies very fast and the future comes upon us almost before we are aware of it. The construction of the great St. Lawrence seaway and the setting up of the Gordon commission has shown that we are very much alive to this fact. In no part of Canada is planning for the future more urgent and more essential than in Newfoundland, because not only must we close the very substantial gap between our standard of living and that of the mainland of Canada, but we must also at the same time make confederation an economic reality. At the present time confederation is merely a political fact. It will become an economic reality only when Newfoundland has been fully integrated into the Canadian economy.
As we project ourselves 20 or 25 years into the future, we see that we can expect

to have a population of from 700,000 to
800.000	people. The resources of our provinces must therefore be developed to provide jobs and wealth that will support these
800.000	people with a standard of living comparable to that which will obtain on the mainland 20 years hence. The distribution of that population will be determined largely by the distribution of the natural resources that are to be developed. Transportation will therefore play a vital role.
Three questions naturally arise. First, is our present system of transportation adequate to the task that it will be called upon to perform? The second question is: If not, is it capable of being transformed and made adequate through improvement? The third question is: If this is impossible, what should be done?
In my opinion, the present system is not adequate and can never become adequate to the task of integrating the economy of the province of Newfoundland with that of the mainland of Canada to such a degree as will permit the province to assimilate and support 800,000 people in the next 25 years. The reason for this appears to me to be very simple. Our present transportation was never intended to do that job. It was not built with that in mind, and therefore it cannot be satisfactorily adapted.
During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Newfoundland developed as an economic sociological adjunct of Great Britain. People settled in St. John's and along the northeast coast, and all the large settlements had direct ties with the west of England. During the period of 1900 to 1950, these ties with the old country gradually weakened, and along the south and west coasts there began to develop ties with the United States and with the mainland of Canada. St. John's, however, during that period, retained and partly strengthened its position as the economic hub of our province, particularly when a tenuous system of land transportation began to develop with the opening of the railway and the building of the road system.
That was all right as long as Newfoundland was looking eastward. With confederation, however, have come modifications of our channels of commerce. Trade with mainland Canada increased from $40 million in 1939 to over $150 million at the present time. St. John's, which for centuries was the front door and the principal exporting and importing centre, has now become the back door of our island. Instead of being our nearest point of contact to the country with which we have most in common politically and economically, it has now become our most inaccessible point in the whole province from 67509-1184
Committee on Railways and Shipping the point of view of our new political and commercial ties, which have resulted from confederation.
Like Gaul, Newfoundland is divided into three physiographic units, each of which has some important subdivisions that have developed more or less as economic entities. The first of these units may be called the west coast area, which can be represented on a map by a line drawn from the bottom of La Poile bay on the southwest coast to the bottom of Green bay on the northeast coast. The second unit is the central portion of the island, which lies east of the line I have just described to the isthmus of Avalon. The third unit is the Avalon peninsula itself.
The economic centre of the west coast area is Corner Brook, which with its main industry dominates and at the same time provides the' hub of the economy of this region. An important subdivision of this area is the-St. George's bay area, which stretches south far enough to include Port aux Basques. The importance and independence of this subdivision has been accentuated in recent years by the United States defence installations. This whole unit has developed an economy which to a large extent is independent of the rest of the province. The high and rugged land stretching from La Poile to Cape St. John makes the development of a transportation system between the west coast and the rest of the island very difficult and most costly.
In the northern part of the central portion, the economy is dominated by the Labrador and inshore fisheries, by the sawmill and paper development at Grand Falls and by the mining operations at Buchans. Here again there is a large measure of independence from St. John's.
